solution:
A non-zero imaginary number has the form \(bi\) with \(b \neq 0\) real. Its square \(-b^2\) is negative, and it is never a real number. Complex numbers have no order, so an imaginary number is neither positive nor negative: \(2i\) and \(-3i\) cannot be compared with \(0\) by size. Only the claim that it is always positive is not a property of an imaginary number.

Hence (D).
note: fit-check flag settled: Key D is right: imaginary numbers are not ordered, so they are neither positive nor negative; the solution wrongly calls them positive or negative.

solution:
Conjugation reflects the point about the real axis, so for any \(z\) that is not a negative real number, \(\text{Arg}(\bar{z}) = -\text{Arg}(z)\). (For a negative real \(z\), the principal argument is \(\pi\) for both \(z\) and \(\bar{z}\), so the rule holds only up to \(2\pi\) there.) The other options fail in general: for \(z=1\), \(\pi+\text{Arg}(z) = \pi\) and \(2\,\text{Arg}(z)=0\) are not equal to \(\text{Arg}(\bar z)=0\) in the same way, and \(z=i\) gives \(\text{Arg}(\bar z) = -\pi/2 \neq \text{Arg}(z)\).

Hence (A).
note: fit-check flag settled: Key A is the only fitting option, but the stored claim fails for negative real z, where both arguments equal pi (principal value).

solution:
Combine the fractions: \(S = \dfrac{(1-\omega^2)+(1-\omega)}{(1-\omega)(1-\omega^2)} = \dfrac{2-(\omega+\omega^2)}{(1-\omega)(1-\omega^2)}\).

Using \(1+\omega+\omega^2=0\), we get \(\omega+\omega^2=-1\), so the numerator is \(2-(-1)=3\).

The denominator is \(1-\omega-\omega^2+\omega^3 = 1-(-1)+1 = 3\).

So \(S = \dfrac{3}{3} = 1\).

Hence (A).
note: fit-check flag settled: (1-w)(1-w^2) = 1 - w - w^2 + w^3 = 3, not 1+w+w^2 (which is 0). Numerator 2-(w+w^2) = 3, so S = 1.

solution:
Let \(|z|=1\) and \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).

(A) \(\text{Arg}(z^n) = n\,\text{Arg}(z)\) up to a multiple of \(2\pi\), so it holds modulo the principal range.

(B) \(|z^n| = |z|^n = 1\) for every integer \(n\).

(C) \(z\bar{z} = |z|^2 = 1\), which holds here because \(|z|=1\).

All three statements are true, so the answer is 'all of the above'.

Hence (D).
note: fit-check flag settled: All three hold when |z|=1, but z times conj(z) = |z|^2, which equals 1 only because |z|=1; the solution says it holds for any z.

solution:
For \(z=x+iy \neq 0\), \(\dfrac{z}{\bar z} = \dfrac{z^2}{|z|^2} = \dfrac{x^2-y^2+2ixy}{x^2+y^2}\), which is real only when \(xy=0\), that is, when \(z\) is real or purely imaginary. For example, \(z=1+i\) gives \(i\), which is not real. So (B) is not true for all \(z \neq 0\).

The others always hold: \(|z|=0 \Leftrightarrow z=0\); \(|z_1 z_2| = |z_1||z_2|\); \(|z| \ge 0\).

Hence (B).
note: fit-check flag settled: Key B is right, but z/conj(z) = z^2/|z|^2 is real exactly when xy = 0, not only when y = 0 (z = i gives -1).
